video_title: Lawfare Daily: ‘The Russian General Staff’ with Oscar Jonsson
gist: Oscar Jonsson, author of 'The Russian General Staff', argues Russia's general staff has evolved from a politically assertive institution into a subordinated yes-man whose expertise did not shape the 2014 Crimea or 2022 Ukraine decisions, which were driven by the security services. He outlines Russian theory (non-contact warfare, non-military means, attrition), says Russia's strike campaign is its main bet as the West runs out of Patriot interceptors, and warns that readiness-based forecasts of Russia's next war and hopes that a Ukraine ceasefire ends the confrontation are misguided.

themes.theme: General staff structure vs US joint staff

insights.claim: Russia's general staff is a permanent professional caste: top officers are pulled from the army, navy and air force in their late 20s/early 30s, trained in general staff academies, and then fill leading positions across the armed forces, unlike the rotational US Joint Chiefs model.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Western analysts mirror-imaging Russia's general staff onto the US Joint Chiefs will misread who actually commands Russian forces.
insights.quote: it's basically its own profession, more or less its own branch within the Russian armed forces

insights.claim: The Russian general staff numbers roughly 10,000 people versus about 1,500 on the US Joint Staff, and unlike the US chairman (an adviser outside the operational chain) it sits atop the operational command architecture of military districts and joint strategic commands.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Scale and command authority make the general staff the center of Russian military planning and theory, a key node to monitor.
insights.quote: the general staff in the Russian system which is I mean maybe 10,000 in in in total or such whereas the the joint staff in the US is around 1500

insights.claim: Jonsson argues the general staff is understudied in the West precisely because it differs so much from Western equivalents; he found almost no literature on it beyond a few articles and books over 20 years old.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Analytical blind spots on Russian institutions create mispriced risk assessments of Russian military behavior.

themes.theme: Political subordination and the loss of candid military advice

insights.claim: Putin moved early to control the military by installing his KGB associate Sergei Ivanov as defense minister and in 2004 reversed Yeltsin's arrangement under which the chief of general staff reported directly to the president, placing the general staff back under the defense minister despite opposition from military heavyweights.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Shows the long-run design of Putin's system: civilian loyalists over the uniformed military.

insights.claim: 2008 is the last case Jonsson finds of a Russian chief of general staff openly criticizing political leadership; after the dismissal of Yuri Baluyevsky the general staff stopped taking political fights and became a loyal servant.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Russian military leadership is no longer a check on political risk-taking, raising tail risk of poorly reasoned escalation.
insights.quote: since then the Russian general staff had just not had that that self-confidence they're not taking political fights

insights.claim: Historically the general staff did push back: it opposed the 1979 Afghanistan intervention and the first Chechen war, with 500-plus sackings and 500-plus resignations around the latter, so today's yes-man posture is a change, not a constant.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: The erosion of military pushback is a structural regime shift worth tracking for any change back.

insights.claim: A 2013 tasking for the general staff to plan the wartime organization of the entire Russian state sparked a seven-year power struggle with other power ministries and ended with the military getting only coordination, not command, authority over agencies like the FSB.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Even as Russia's military instrument grows, the military's political clout is shrinking; security services retain primacy.
insights.quote: Like you can you can call someone and you say, "Hey, you know, screw you." And then you have coordinated.

insights.claim: Jonsson's core thesis is a paradox: a vastly expanding Russian military instrument coexists with dramatically decreasing political influence of the top military leadership, culminating in yes-manship that produces bad policy.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Forecasting Russian behavior from military capability alone misses that decisions are made by a narrow, security-service-dominated circle.
insights.quote: on the one hand you have an a vastly expanding military instrument but at the same time you have a a dramatically decreasing political influence from the Russian top military leadership

themes.theme: Who decided Crimea and the 2022 invasion

insights.claim: The 2014 Crimea decision was made by current and former FSB directors — Putin, Nikolai Patrushev and Alexander Bortnikov — with some defense-ministry involvement under Shoigu, but Jonsson finds no evidence the general staff shaped the decision.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Russian war decisions originate in the security services, so intelligence-service signals matter more than military signals.

insights.claim: EU and US sanctions after Crimea support this reading: FSB figures, Shoigu's aides and the GRU head were sanctioned for Crimea, while the chief of general staff was sanctioned only for the force buildup on Ukraine's border.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Sanctions designations can serve as a revealed-preference map of Western intelligence views on who drives Russian decisions.

insights.claim: The 2022 invasion was a security-services plan premised on a coup and a 10-day war with about 120,000 troops; the general staff knew Russia's mobilization army, missing roughly 30% mobilized personnel and 30% conscripts, would field hollow units without infantry, yet said nothing publicly.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Military rationale did not drive the most consequential Russian decision in decades; capability-based forecasts of Russian action are unreliable.
insights.quote: it was a you know security services plan by you know we're going to walk in there with a coup d'etat we're not going to face uh serious resistance it's going to be over in 10 days

insights.claim: Russia now has over 700,000 men in the war in Ukraine, versus roughly 120,000 at the start of the 2022 invasion, which French military intelligence had judged too few for a real war.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: The war has become a mass-mobilization attrition contest, far beyond initial planning assumptions.
insights.quote: today Russia's over 700,000 men in the war

insights.claim: Formally the GRU sits under the chief of general staff, but unlike the SVR and FSB it lacks daily briefings with Putin and has no permanent seat on the weekly Security Council, where the chief of general staff has only a non-permanent seat.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Institutional access signals which agencies shape Kremlin decisions.

insights.claim: Jonsson's best guess is that the GRU's classic military intelligence and spetsnaz functions run through the general staff, while its political war against the West — poisonings in the UK, killings in Berlin — is planned and green-lit at the political level, not by the chief of general staff.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Sabotage and assassination campaigns in Europe should be read as Kremlin political decisions, not military-bureaucratic drift.
insights.quote: if you're going to go poison some Russian dissident in the UK or, you know, shoot a chain in in Berlin, etc., you know, it's not the chief of general staff who draws up those plans

themes.theme: Russian military theory: non-contact war, non-military means, attrition

insights.claim: Russia sees the West's strategy as winning through non-military means — sanctions, political isolation, indirect support to Ukraine, information and intelligence operations — and believes it is currently working, which is why Russia is escalating intelligence and subversion operations in Europe to 'flip the table'.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Expect rising Russian sabotage/subversion activity in Europe as Russia's position weakens; a risk factor for European infrastructure and assets.
insights.quote: They need to do something to flip the table.

insights.claim: Russian doctrine treats Ukraine as a mere manifestation of a broader conflict with the West, which Moscow believes is using Ukraine to cause regime collapse in Russia.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: A Ukraine ceasefire would not end Russia-West confrontation; risk would shift elsewhere rather than disappear.
insights.quote: They're seeing Ukraine just as a mere manifestation of a broader conflict with the West.

insights.claim: The 1991 Gulf War, where Iraq's Soviet equipment and doctrine were routed by US situational awareness and long-range precision strike, is the single most important theme in Russian military theory of the last 30 years, spawning Vladimir Slipchenko's 'non-contact warfare' concept.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Explains Russia's heavy investment in long-range strike and its fear of a Western aerospace first strike.

insights.claim: Russia's pre-war doctrine of 'active defense' assumed NATO would open with a massive aerospace attack to decapitate leadership; Russia's plan was to survive the initial period and then win by attrition because NATO production rates and magazine depth only allow short wars — an approach Jonsson says resembles what Iran did after strikes this spring.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Western magazine depth and munitions production capacity are a core strategic vulnerability Russia explicitly plans to exploit; supports defense-industrial investment theses.
insights.quote: NATO production rates and NATO magazine depth only allows for a short and victorious wars

insights.claim: Makhmut Gareev's backward-looking view that Russia wins wars through mobilization and industrial production, not Slipchenko's futurism, became the de facto Russian strategy after the early phase of the 2022 war turned into attrition.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Russia's war is a production race; industrial output figures are the key indicator to watch.

themes.theme: Strikes, interceptors and the war's trajectory

insights.claim: Jonsson argues 'strikes does not equal strategy': strategic bombing rarely produces decisive advantage in a relevant time frame, as shown by Iran (great strikes, no political win) and by over four years of Russian bombing of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of narratives that air or missile campaigns alone will force political outcomes.

insights.claim: Russia is losing territory with record casualties on the front line, so its strike campaign against Ukrainian critical infrastructure, industry and economic potential is its best and almost only bet to win, and will cause more severe damage this winter.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Watch Ukrainian energy and industrial infrastructure damage this winter; front-line gains are unlikely to be Russia's path.
insights.quote: They're actually losing territory with record casualties in the front line

insights.claim: Ukraine is intercepting around 0% of Russian ballistic missiles because the West is out of Patriot interceptors, depleted in part by the US and partners burning them in the Middle East, while cheap cruise missiles and jet drones have no cost-efficient defense.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Interceptor shortages are acute; strong demand signal for air-defense producers and cheap counter-drone/counter-missile solutions.
insights.quote: Ukraine is intercepting basically around 0% of Russian ballistic missiles because we're out of Patriot interceptors

themes.theme: Implications for Western policy and readiness

insights.claim: European intelligence forecasts that Russia will be ready for a new war in 3, 5 or 7 years rest on reconstitution assumptions that Jonsson says are flawed, because Russian war decisions do not follow military expertise or readiness.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Timelines for Russia-NATO conflict risk keyed to Russian rearmament may be misleading; political decision mechanics matter more.
insights.quote: we need to do away with all those projections of of Russia being ready in one or two or three years

insights.claim: Provocatively, Jonsson suggests Russia's most relevant capability window may be now — with zero Patriot interceptors available across the West and Russia producing around 720 ballistic missiles a year — rather than later when European defense spending starts to deliver.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Near-term European security risk may be higher than consensus; supports urgency in air-defense procurement.
insights.quote: Russia produces around 720 ballistic missile a year

insights.claim: A ceasefire in Ukraine would not change European or transatlantic security, because Russian theory sees NATO and the West as the enemy; Russian energy would simply be redirected elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Don't price a Ukraine ceasefire as a durable de-escalation; European defense demand should persist.
insights.quote: if you have a ceasefire in Ukraine, you know, nothing's going to change for for European or transatlantic security

insights.claim: Gulf States disregarded the threat from cheap one-way attack drones for four years despite the evidence, and Western militaries are still failing to internalize even simple, openly available lessons on new technologies.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Adoption lag on counter-drone and cheap mass technologies creates both vulnerability and procurement upside for vendors that address it.
insights.quote: we saw Gulf States completely disregarding the threat from cheap oneway attack drones for 4 years

insights.claim: Sweden and Finland have stronger Russia-studies traditions than most, with Sweden keeping Russia research programs alive even in peaceful years, but Jonsson says expertise exists in 'islands' that political and military leaders often do not act on.
insights.speaker: Oscar Jonsson
insights.so_what: Expert warnings do not translate automatically into policy; lag in policy response is a persistent pattern.
